blocks.text: Predictive modelling uses data to predict future outcomes: machine learning models analyse patterns in past data to estimate what may happen next. Predictions support planning and decisions in many fields, but they are based on probability and do not always explain why something happens, so understanding causality is also important.

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Give examples such as weather prediction, and ask whether a prediction explains the cause. Discuss the difference.

Predictive outcomes are the results a trained model produces from past data: estimates of future values or events. Their accuracy depends on data quality and good training. Businesses use predictions to forecast markets and sales; healthcare uses them in diagnosis.

Causality explains why an event happens: a cause-and-effect relationship in which one factor directly influences another. It is important in scientific studies. Data alone may not show causality; experiments, which change one factor while keeping others fixed, often identify causes. Understanding causes improves decisions and avoids false assumptions.

blocks.caption: Prediction and causation
rows: Cause-and-effect relationships, often shown by experiments
A student's final grade from previous marks, attendance and study hours; tomorrow's temperature from past weather
Regular study hours improving exam performance; smoking increasing the risk of lung disease
Sales forecasting, stock trends, disease risk, student performance
Choosing actions that will actually change an outcome

blocks.text: A model can predict accurately without understanding the underlying causes. For example, ice-cream sales and drowning cases may rise together in summer: one predicts the other, but hot weather causes both. Knowing the cause matters when deciding what to change.

blocks.alt: Left panel, prediction (what will happen?): past data such as marks and attendance goes into a model, which gives a forecast of the likely final grade; it can be accurate without knowing the reason. Right panel, causation (why does it happen?): a cause, regular study hours, has an arrow to an effect, better grades; causes are shown by experiments that change one factor and keep others fixed, for example smoking causing lung disease; two things rising together is not enough to prove cause.
blocks.caption: Prediction and causation (original diagram after 6.9).
blocks.long_description: Prediction answers 'what next?' and causation answers 'why?'; good decisions usually need both.

blocks.prompt: A model finds that students who own more books get higher marks. Does this prove that buying books raises marks? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. It shows a pattern useful for prediction, not a cause. Other factors, such as family support or time spent reading, could cause both; an experiment that changes only the number of books would be needed to show causation.

items: Prediction estimates what may happen from past patterns.
Causation explains why: cause and effect, often shown by experiments.
Patterns that move together are not proof of cause.
